Git becomes much easier when you stop treating it as a bag of commands.

Think of it as a **graph of snapshots**.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key ideas
`repository` `working tree` `staging area` `commit` `branch`
`HEAD` `merge` `rebase` `remote` `fetch` `pull` `push`
:::

## The three places

```text
Working directory
      │ git add
      ▼
Staging area
      │ git commit
      ▼
Repository history
```

A basic rhythm:

```bash
git status
git add analysis.py
git commit -m "Add bootstrap analysis"
git log --oneline
```

## Best resources

**Pro Git — free official book:**  
https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2

**Git Reference:**  
https://git-scm.com/docs

**Learn Git Branching — visual and interactive:**  
https://learngitbranching.js.org/

**GitHub's Introduction to Git:**  
https://github.com/skills/introduction-to-git

## Practice visually

Use Learn Git Branching to see:

```text
A──B──C  main
    \
     D──E  experiment
```

Commands such as merge and rebase make far more sense when you can visualize the commit graph.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Git is also a recovery system
Before using destructive-looking commands copied from the internet, understand what will happen to the working tree, index and commit graph. `git status` is your friend.
:::
